title: The message comes from the shell binary itself, not su
explanation: `su - ci -c 'echo ok'` prints `This account is currently not available.` That exact wording is `/usr/sbin/nologin`'s own canned output — su successfully started a session and handed control to whatever program is configured as ci's shell, and that program's entire job is to print this message and exit nonzero.

title: Confirm the configured shell directly
explanation: `getent passwd ci` shows the account's last field — its login shell — is `/usr/sbin/nologin`. That's a deliberate, working lockout mechanism, correctly installed and functioning exactly as designed; the account was 'hardened' by pointing it there.

title: nologin is right for accounts that never need a shell, wrong for ones that do
explanation: `nologin` is the standard way to prevent interactive login for accounts like `daemon` or `nobody` that should never get a shell. But `su - <user>`, cron's `su` wrappers, and any login-shell automation all route through the account's configured shell too — if that automation is how `ci` is actually meant to run jobs, `nologin` blocks the legitimate use case along with the illegitimate one.

title: Restore a real, executable shell
explanation: `sudo usermod -s /bin/bash ci` points the account back at an actual shell binary capable of running commands, rather than one whose only behavior is to refuse and exit.

title: Verify with the same command that failed
explanation: Re-running `su - ci -c 'echo ok'` and seeing `ok` confirms the account can now actually execute something — not just that `getent passwd` reports a different shell field.
